name: Adidas Adizero Adios 10
description: The tenth edition of Adidas's classic lightweight racing flat, continuing the low-stack Lightstrike Pro formula of the Adios 9. It targets runners who prefer a fast, firm, unplated shoe for intervals, tempos, and 5K-10K racing. A rare traditional flat in a market full of tall super trainers.
pros: Light and responsive for speed work
Good value for a fast shoe
cons: Firm ride is not for everyone

name: Adidas Adizero Adios 9
description: A traditional low-profile speed shoe with Lightstrike Pro under the forefoot and a firm, connected ride. It is a throwback flat that shines for track sessions, tempo runs, and shorter races without a plate. Suits runners who want ground feel rather than a tall super-shoe stack.
cons: Too firm for long easy miles

name: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4
description: Adidas's flagship marathon racer with a full Lightstrike Pro midsole and Energyrods 2.0 glass-fiber-infused carbon rods. The ride is bouncy and aggressive, rewarding runners who can hold marathon pace or faster. One of the top-tier super shoes for half marathon and marathon race day.
pros: Highly propulsive rocker at race pace
Lighter than most rivals in its class
cons: Expensive and durability is only fair

name: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5
description: The next iteration of Adidas's Lightstrike Pro and Energyrods marathon super shoe, refining the Adios Pro 4 formula. Built for full-effort half marathons and marathons with an aggressive forward-rolling ride. Best for efficient midfoot and forefoot strikers chasing PRs.
pros: Light and aggressive at fast paces
cons: Not meant for easy daily miles

name: Adidas Adizero Boston 13
description: A plated training workhorse that pairs Lightstrike Pro with Energyrods for uptempo daily miles. The 13 borrows heavily from the Evo SL's geometry, making it smoother and less harsh than earlier Bostons. It works as a one-shoe solution for runners who mix easy miles with workouts.
pros: Versatile from easy pace to tempo
Energyrods add pop without racer harshness

name: Adidas Adizero Boston 14
description: The follow-up to the Boston 13, keeping the Lightstrike Pro plus Energyrods recipe for plated everyday training. It sits between a daily trainer and a race shoe, favoring runners who like a firm, rolling ride at moderate to fast paces. A dependable pick for marathon training blocks.
pros: Handles workouts and daily miles alike
cons: Not as soft as max-cushion trainers
A touch heavy for race day

name: Adidas Adizero Evo SL
description: A plateless super trainer with a full slab of Lightstrike Pro foam in the Adios Pro Evo silhouette. It delivers a bouncy, fast, fun ride at a remarkable weight and price, which made it one of the most hyped shoes of 2025. Great for everything from easy days to workouts and even racing on a budget.
pros: Very light for a max-stack trainer
cons: Less stable for pronounced heel strikers
Thin outsole coverage wears faster than the Boston

name: Adidas Adizero Evo SL 2
description: The sequel to the breakout Evo SL, keeping the full Lightstrike Pro midsole and plate-free super-trainer formula. It aims at runners who want one light, bouncy shoe for daily training, workouts, and long runs. Expect the same fast-rolling ride with refinements to the upper and outsole.
pros: Top-shelf foam without a super-shoe price
cons: Not the most stable at easy jogs
High demand can make it hard to find

name: Adidas Adizero Prime X 4
description: The continuation of Adidas's rule-breaking Prime X line, stacking Lightstrike Pro past the legal limit with Energyrods for maximum propulsion. It suits long marathon-pace efforts and runners chasing the biggest possible cushioning, not sanctioned races. A statement shoe that trades stability for bounce.
pros: Maximum cushioning in the Adidas lineup
cons: Heavy and unwieldy for a plated shoe

name: Adidas Adizero Prime X Evo
description: An over-the-limit super shoe with roughly 50mm of Lightstrike Pro and Energyrods, exceeding World Athletics stack rules. It is a maximal training and fun-run tool rather than a legal racer, giving huge bounce on long efforts. Best for experienced runners who want the most shoe possible under foot.

name: Adidas Adizero SL2
description: The budget-friendly entry point to the Adizero line, pairing Lightstrike 2.0 foam with a Lightstrike Pro insert under the forefoot. It is a no-frills, slightly firm daily trainer that can pick up the pace when needed. A solid value pick for new runners or as a mileage shoe in a rotation.

name: Adidas Adizero Takumi Sen 10
description: A featherweight 5K-10K racer with Lightstrike Pro and short Energyrods under the forefoot. The low, aggressive platform demands an efficient stride and quick turnover, making it a specialist rather than an all-rounder. It is a favorite for road mile to 10K racing and hard interval sessions.
cons: Too little shoe for most marathoners
Narrow fit will not suit wide feet

name: Adidas Adizero Takumi Sen 12
description: The latest in Adidas's short-distance racing line, continuing the Takumi Sen recipe of Lightstrike Pro foam with forefoot Energyrods. It is built for 5K and 10K race pace, hard track and road workouts, and runners with quick, efficient strides. Expect a firm, snappy, very light ride.

name: Adidas Supernova Prima
description: The max-cushion member of the Supernova family, with a tall Dreamstrike+ midsole for plush easy miles. It is built for recovery days, high-mileage comfort, and bigger runners who want more foam underfoot. Think of it as Adidas's answer to the Nimbus and More Foam class.
pros: Stable base for a tall trainer
cons: Heavy and slow to turn over

name: Adidas Supernova Rise 2
description: Adidas's mainstream daily trainer with Dreamstrike+ foam and support rods that give a stable, comfortable ride. It is aimed at everyday runners logging easy and steady miles rather than the Adizero speed crowd. A dependable, well-priced workhorse comparable to the Pegasus and Ghost.

name: Adidas Supernova Rise 3
description: The third generation of Adidas's core daily trainer, continuing the Dreamstrike+ midsole and stable, easygoing ride of the Rise 2. It targets everyday mileage, from recovery jogs to weekend long runs, for a wide range of runners. A safe first recommendation at a fair price.
pros: Stable without being a stability shoe
cons: Ride can feel plain next to super trainers

name: Adidas Supernova Solution
description: The stability entry in the Supernova line, adding firmer medial support rods to the Dreamstrike+ platform. It serves runners who overpronate or simply want guided, secure daily miles. A straightforward alternative to the Adrenaline GTS and GT-2000 at a similar price.
cons: Support may feel intrusive for neutral runners

name: Adidas Ultraboost 5
description: The latest Ultraboost pairs Light Boost foam with a knit upper for a comfortable, springy ride that leans lifestyle as much as running. It works for easy miles, walking, and all-day wear, but serious training is better served by the Supernova or Adizero lines. Its popularity comes largely from comfort and style.
cons: Dense ride lacks pop for workouts

name: Altra Escalante 4
description: Altra's classic zero-drop street shoe pairs a low stack of Ego foam with a stretchy knit upper and the brand's roomiest Original footshape toe box. It's a flexible, ground-feel trainer for natural-running fans, easy miles, and all-day wear.
pros: Doubles as a comfortable casual shoe

name: Altra Escalante 5
description: The fifth Escalante keeps Altra's signature combination of zero drop, a low Ego foam stack, and a sock-like knit upper in the widest Original footshape fit. It remains the go-to for runners who want ground feel and toe splay in a daily shoe.
cons: Knit upper lacks lockdown for speed

name: Altra FWD Experience
description: Altra's first-ever non-zero-drop shoe adds a gentle 4mm offset and a rockered midsole while keeping the roomy foot-shaped toe box. It's a friendly gateway for runners who like Altra's fit but aren't ready for a flat platform.
pros: Easiest entry into the Altra fit
Roomy toe box without full zero drop
cons: Purists may prefer true zero drop

name: Altra FWD Via
description: The FWD Via is Altra's plush high-stack cruiser with a 4mm drop, a big rockered slab of Ego Max foam, and a wide, stable base. It brings max cushioning and the signature roomy toe box to runners who found the Via Olympus's zero drop too demanding.
pros: Plush cushioning with a roomy toe box
Gentle drop eases the transition from conventional shoes
cons: Rocker feels clunky at quicker paces

name: Altra Paradigm 7
description: Altra's stability trainer combines a full 30mm of Ego Max foam with GuideRail-style support pods and the widest Original footshape fit. It's one of very few options for overpronators who want zero drop and serious toe room in a supportive package.
cons: Support pods feel intrusive to neutral runners

name: Altra Torin 8
description: Altra's flagship cushioned daily trainer runs a 30mm slab of soft Ego Max foam under the whole foot with the brand's Standard footshape fit. It's the most conventional-feeling entry point to zero drop, comfortable for everything from recovery jogs to long runs.
pros: Best all-rounder in Altra's road line

name: Altra Torin 9
description: The Torin 9 carries forward Altra's balanced zero-drop daily trainer with Ego Max cushioning and a foot-shaped toe box. It stays the safest recommendation for runners moving into low-drop shoes who still want real cushioning underfoot.
pros: Easy transition shoe into zero drop

name: Altra Vanish Carbon 2
description: The only true zero-drop carbon racer on the market pairs Altra's Ego Pro foam with a full-length carbon plate in a slimmed-down footshape fit. It gives midfoot and forefoot strikers a fast, roomy-toed race option no other brand offers.
cons: Zero drop is demanding over a marathon
Less foam than top-tier super shoes

name: ASICS Gel-Cumulus 27
description: ASICS's everyday neutral workhorse, sitting below the Nimbus with a lighter, more balanced FF Blast Plus Eco midsole. It is unspectacular in the best way: enough cushion for daily miles without the weight or price of the flagship. A sensible one-shoe option for new and moderate-mileage runners.
pros: Good value for a premium-feeling trainer

name: ASICS Gel-Cumulus 28
description: The 2026 Cumulus keeps the formula of its predecessor: a moderate stack of FF Blast Plus Eco foam in a light, accommodating package for daily training. It stays the sensible middle option in the ASICS lineup for runners who find the Nimbus too much shoe.

name: ASICS Gel-Kayano 32
description: The benchmark premium stability trainer, pairing soft FF Blast Plus Eco foam with ASICS's 4D Guidance System instead of a hard medial post. It guides overpronators gently while still feeling plush, making it a go-to for runners who need support over high mileage. It is protective rather than quick.

name: ASICS Gel-Kayano 33
description: The 2026 Kayano carries forward the FF Blast Plus Eco midsole and 4D Guidance System formula that made recent versions the standard for plush stability. Expect the same supportive, high-cushion ride for overpronators logging daily and long-run miles, with minor upper and weight refinements.
pros: Fits a wide range of runners
cons: Premium price for a daily trainer

name: ASICS Gel-Nimbus 27
description: ASICS's flagship max-cushion cruiser, built on a tall slab of FF Blast Plus Eco foam with a plush knit collar. It is a soft, protective shoe for easy miles and recovery days rather than anything fast. Heavier runners and heel strikers who want maximum protection are the target audience.
cons: Too soft and slow-feeling for workouts

name: ASICS Gel-Nimbus 28
description: The 2026 update to ASICS's max-cushion flagship keeps the tall FF Blast Plus Eco midsole and plush upper while trimming a little weight. It remains a soft, high-protection shoe for easy days, long slow runs, and runners who prioritize comfort over speed.

name: ASICS GT-1000 13
description: The entry point to ASICS stability, with FF Blast cushioning and light medial guidance at a hundred-dollar price. It gives newer runners and mild overpronators a supportive, no-frills daily trainer. The foam is simpler and firmer than the pricier GT-2000 and Kayano.
cons: Lacks the refinement of pricier siblings

name: ASICS GT-1000 15
description: The 2026 version of ASICS's budget stability trainer, continuing the FF Blast midsole and light guidance setup of the GT-1000 13. It stays the value pick for mild overpronators who want dependable support for everyday miles without spending trainer-flagship money.

name: ASICS GT-2000 13
description: The mid-priced stability staple in the ASICS line, using FF Blast Plus foam and a 3D Guidance System to steady overpronators without a rigid post. It is lighter and cheaper than the Kayano while covering the same daily-training territory. A dependable pick for runners who need support but not maximum plushness.
pros: Lighter and cheaper than the Kayano

name: ASICS GT-2000 15
description: The 2026 edition of ASICS's mid-tier stability trainer, expected to continue the FF Blast Plus midsole and guidance-based support of recent versions. It remains the value-minded alternative to the Kayano for overpronators who want a lighter everyday shoe.
pros: Balanced stability at a fair price

name: ASICS Hyper Speed 3
description: A plateless, no-frills lightweight racer built on simple FlyteFoam at a bargain price. It is the old-school racing-flat experience: low, light, and flexible, rewarding efficient form at 5K-to-half-marathon efforts. Ideal for budget racers, track workouts, and runners who dislike plated stiffness.
pros: Excellent price for a race shoe
Great for intervals and shorter races
cons: Basic foam with modest energy return
Too little cushion for most marathoners

name: ASICS Hyper Speed 6
description: The 2026 entry in ASICS's budget racing line keeps the recipe simple: a light, plateless FlyteFoam package for fast workouts and races at a fraction of super-shoe cost. It remains a workhorse flat for speed sessions and shorter race distances.
pros: Cheapest true speed shoe in the lineup
cons: Not a marathon shoe for most

name: ASICS Magic Speed 4
description: A budget-friendly carbon-plated speed shoe with a full-length plate sandwiched between FF Turbo Plus and FF Blast Plus foam. It delivers much of the snap of a super shoe at nearly half the price, making it a smart workout companion and an honest race option for runners who don't want to burn a Metaspeed. The ride is firmer and less forgiving than true top-tier racers.
pros: Carbon-plate propulsion at a fair price
cons: Snug fit won't suit wide feet

name: ASICS Magic Speed 5
description: The 2026 Magic Speed continues the value super-shoe formula: a full carbon plate between layers of FF Turbo Plus and FF Blast Plus foam. It stays the workout-day plated shoe in the ASICS range and a legitimate racer for runners who want plate benefits without Metaspeed pricing.
pros: Tough enough for repeated tempo sessions

name: ASICS Metaspeed Edge 4
description: The 2026 cadence-style Metaspeed carries forward the Tokyo edition's carbon plate and FF Leap foam with an 8mm drop tuned for fast turnover. It stays the pick within ASICS's racing line for runners who increase step rate rather than stride length when pushing pace.
pros: Snappy plate geometry for cadence runners
cons: Incremental change from the Tokyo edition

name: ASICS Metaspeed Edge Paris
description: The cadence-runner counterpart to the Sky Paris, using the same carbon plate and FF Turbo Plus foam but with a higher 8mm drop and a plate geometry tuned for quick turnover. The ride is snappier and slightly firmer than the Sky, rewarding runners who speed up by increasing step rate. Many amateurs actually find it the more usable of the two racers.
cons: Firm ride over the final marathon miles

name: ASICS Metaspeed Edge Tokyo
description: The cadence-style Tokyo racer pairs new FF Leap foam with a carbon plate tuned for rapid turnover and an 8mm drop. It keeps the Edge's snappy, controlled character while getting lighter and springier than the Paris generation. A top-shelf choice for racers who run fast by upping their step rate.
pros: Works for a wider range of strikes than the Sky

name: ASICS Metaspeed Sky 4
description: The 2026 generation of the stride-style Metaspeed racer, continuing the carbon plate and ultralight FF Leap-based platform of the Tokyo edition. It remains ASICS's flagship marathon shoe for runners who extend their stride at race pace.
cons: Specs largely carried over from the Tokyo edition

name: ASICS Metaspeed Sky Paris
description: ASICS's 2024 flagship marathon racer for stride-style runners, with a full-length carbon plate in ultralight FF Turbo Plus foam. It is exceptionally light, aggressively bouncy, and built for runners who lengthen their stride as they speed up. One of the most decorated super shoes of its generation.
pros: Big compliant bounce for bounding strides
cons: Less suited to pronounced heel strikers

name: ASICS Metaspeed Sky Tokyo
description: The 2025 Tokyo edition upgrades the stride-runner Metaspeed with ASICS's new top-tier FF Leap foam over the carbon plate, adding bounce while cutting weight. It is even lighter and more energetic than the Paris version, aimed squarely at marathon and half-marathon PRs. Price climbed along with the performance.
pros: Lighter and bouncier than the Paris edition
Excellent energy return from FF Leap foam

name: ASICS Noosa Tri 15
description: A triathlon-bred lightweight trainer with bouncy FF Blast Plus foam, a sockless-friendly upper, and quick-entry elastic laces. The loud colorways are a signature, but underneath is a genuinely fast, fun shoe for tempo runs, short races, and brick workouts. Runners who never touch a wetsuit still buy it for speed days.
pros: Easy on-off for transitions and comfortable sockless
cons: Low drop can strain heel-striker calves
Thin upper trades structure for speed

name: ASICS Noosa Tri 16
description: The 2025 Noosa keeps the FF Blast Plus midsole, elastic laces, and barefoot-friendly interior that make it the default short-course triathlon shoe. It doubles as a light uptempo trainer for road runners who want something quicker than a daily shoe without going full race flat.
pros: Light and energetic at tempo paces
cons: Not cushioned enough for long easy miles

name: ASICS Noosa Tri 17
description: The 2026 edition of ASICS's long-running triathlon speedster carries forward FF Blast Plus cushioning, stretch laces, and a sockless-ready fit. It stays the go-to for short-course triathletes and a fun tempo-day option for road runners.

name: ASICS Novablast 5
description: One of the best-selling daily trainers anywhere, the Novablast 5 moves to soft, bouncy FF Blast Max foam on a tall trampoline-shaped midsole. It is light for its stack and lively enough to handle everything from easy days to uptempo long runs. Few shoes offer this much fun per dollar.
cons: Tall soft stack can feel unstable in corners

name: ASICS Novablast 6
description: The 2026 follow-up to ASICS's hugely popular do-everything trainer, keeping the tall, bouncy FF Blast Max midsole that made the 5 a bestseller. It remains a light, energetic neutral shoe for daily miles and long runs at a mainstream price.
pros: Light for the cushion on offer

name: ASICS Superblast 2
description: A plateless super-trainer stacking race-grade FF Turbo Plus foam over FF Blast Plus Eco for a huge yet remarkably light platform. It handles long runs, uptempo work, and even daily miles with the same effortless bounce, which is why many runners treat it as a one-shoe quiver. The only real obstacle is the price.
pros: Superb energy return without a plate
Genuinely versatile from easy to tempo
cons: Tall stack won't suit runners wanting ground feel

name: ASICS Superblast 3
description: The third generation of ASICS's cult-favorite super-trainer keeps the massive dual-layer FF Turbo Plus and FF Blast Plus Eco midsole in a light, plateless package. It carries on as the premium everything-shoe for runners who want race-day foam feel in their daily training.
pros: Light and smooth despite the huge stack
Handles a wide range of paces

name: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25
description: The Adrenaline GTS 25 is Brooks's iconic stability trainer, now with nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 and the GuideRails support system that checks excess ankle roll only when needed. It is the safe pick for overpronators logging daily miles who want support without a harsh medial post.
cons: High drop and structure feel dull at pace

name: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 26
description: The Adrenaline GTS 26 refines the best-selling stability formula: DNA Loft v3 cushioning, GuideRails guidance, and a dependable engineered mesh upper. It stays the go-to recommendation for runners who need moderate pronation support in a daily trainer.

name: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 27
description: The Adrenaline GTS 27 continues the long-running stability line with GuideRails support and nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam. Expect the same protective, supportive daily-mileage ride that has kept the Adrenaline a top seller for over two decades.
pros: GuideRails support that engages only when needed
Fits most feet with width options
cons: High drop won't suit forefoot strikers

name: Brooks Ariel GTS 24
description: The Ariel GTS 24 is the women's counterpart to the Beast, delivering Brooks's maximum motion-control support with extended GuideRails on a wide DNA Loft v2 platform. It serves women who severely overpronate or need a stout, roomy trainer for high-support daily miles.

name: Brooks Beast GTS 24
description: The Beast GTS 24 is Brooks's maximum-support motion-control trainer, combining extended GuideRails with a wide, DNA Loft v2 cushioned platform. It is built for severe overpronators and bigger runners who need the most structure a road shoe can offer.
pros: Strongest support in the Brooks lineup
Roomy fit with multiple wide widths
Durable, protective platform for heavier runners
cons: Overbuilt for runners with mild pronation

name: Brooks Ghost 17
description: The Ghost 17 keeps Brooks's best-selling formula: full-length nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 in a smooth, no-surprises daily trainer. It is a high-drop, heel-striker-friendly shoe that handles easy miles and long runs without demanding anything from your form.
cons: Not lively enough for speed work
High 12mm drop won't suit forefoot strikers

name: Brooks Ghost 18
description: The Ghost 18 is a refinement of the Ghost 17 with the same nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 midsole and a lightly updated engineered mesh upper. It remains the default recommendation for new runners and anyone who wants a dependable, protective daily trainer.
pros: Dependable ride for every easy run
Fits most feet, wide sizes available
cons: Plays it safe — little energy return

name: Brooks Ghost AMP
description: The Ghost AMP is a new, more energetic spin on the Ghost platform, pairing a livelier nitrogen-infused midsole with a higher stack than the standard Ghost. It targets runners who love the Ghost fit but want more bounce for long runs and moderate-pace days.
pros: Livelier ride than the standard Ghost
Versatile across easy and moderate paces
cons: Costs more than the proven Ghost
New model with no track record yet

name: Brooks Ghost Max 3
description: The Ghost Max 3 stacks a tall slab of nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 on a wide base with Brooks's GlideRoll rocker for an easy, protective roll-through. The low 6mm drop plus rocker geometry makes it gentle on calves and joints, and the broad platform gives it a stable-neutral feel bigger runners appreciate.
pros: Rocker keeps heavy shoe from feeling sluggish
cons: Soft rocker ride isn't for runners who like ground feel

name: Brooks Ghost Max 4
description: The Ghost Max 4 continues the max-cushion Ghost formula: high-stack DNA Loft v3, GlideRoll rocker, and a wide, stable base at a 6mm drop. It is built for easy days, recovery miles, and runners who want maximum protection in a familiar Brooks fit.

name: Brooks Glycerin 22
description: The Glycerin 22 debuts Brooks's DNA Tuned midsole in the standard Glycerin — larger, softer foam cells in the heel and smaller, responsive cells in the forefoot. The result is a plush premium trainer that soaks up easy and long-run miles while feeling less mushy than earlier Glycerins.
pros: Plush yet controlled DNA Tuned cushioning
Smooth heel landing for high-mileage training
cons: A bit heavy for faster days
Premium price for a daily trainer

name: Brooks Glycerin 22 GTS
description: The Glycerin 22 GTS adds Brooks's GuideRails support system to the plush DNA Tuned platform of the Glycerin 22. It gives overpronators premium max cushioning with unobtrusive guidance that only engages when the ankle rolls inward.

name: Brooks Glycerin 23
description: The Glycerin 23 carries forward the DNA Tuned dual-cell midsole with a lightly refined upper and outsole. It remains Brooks's flagship plush neutral trainer for runners who prioritize step-in comfort and protection across daily and long-run mileage.
pros: Handles daily miles and long runs alike
cons: Small update if you own the 22

name: Brooks Glycerin 23 GTS
description: The Glycerin 23 GTS pairs the plush DNA Tuned midsole with GuideRails holistic support for runners who need pronation control in a premium cushioned trainer. It is one of the most comfortable stability options on the market for easy and long-run days.
pros: Top-tier comfort in a stability shoe
Support that stays out of the way until needed

name: Brooks Glycerin Flex
description: The Glycerin Flex is a new, more flexible take on the Glycerin platform, trading the rigid rockered geometry of the Max models for a softer forefoot flex and a lower 8mm drop. It suits runners who want plush Glycerin comfort with a more natural, less structured ride.
cons: Brand-new model with no track record

name: Brooks Glycerin Max
description: The Glycerin Max was Brooks's first super-stacked trainer, with roughly 45mm of DNA Tuned foam under the heel and an aggressive GlideRoll rocker. It is a big, soft cruiser built for long runs and recovery days when you want maximum protection underfoot.
pros: Rocker makes the tall stack roll smoothly
Softer heel with a more responsive forefoot
cons: Tall stack feels unstable on sharp turns

name: Brooks Glycerin Max 2
description: The Glycerin Max 2 keeps the towering DNA Tuned midsole and GlideRoll rocker of the original while trimming a little weight and cleaning up the upper. It remains Brooks's plushest shoe, aimed at long, easy miles rather than anything fast.
pros: Smoother, slightly lighter than version one
Great for recovery and long easy runs
cons: $200 for a trainer without a plate

name: Brooks Glycerin Max 3
description: The Glycerin Max 3 continues Brooks's super-stack cruiser with DNA Tuned foam and the GlideRoll rocker, with incremental fit and outsole updates. It is for runners who want the most cushioned shoe in the Brooks lineup for long and easy days.
pros: Maximum cushioning in the Brooks range
Durable enough for high weekly volume

name: Brooks Hyperion 3
description: The Hyperion 3 is Brooks's lightweight speed trainer built on nitrogen-infused DNA Flash v2 foam with no plate. It is a low-slung, fast-feeling shoe for intervals, tempos, and shorter races for runners who prefer ground feel over big stacks.
pros: Great ground feel for fast workouts
More affordable than plated speed shoes
cons: Too firm and thin for long easy miles
No plate means less pop than super trainers

name: Brooks Hyperion 4
description: The Hyperion 4 continues Brooks's plate-free speed shoe with DNA Flash v2 foam and a barely-there upper. It targets track workouts, tempo runs, and racers who want a traditional low-profile fast shoe rather than a carbon super shoe.
cons: Niche in an era of plated trainers

name: Brooks Hyperion Elite 4
description: The Hyperion Elite 4 is Brooks's carbon-plated marathon racer with a full 40mm stack of DNA Flash v2 foam. It is a legal race-day shoe with a firmer, more stable ride than the bounciest super shoes, suiting runners who want predictability over maximum squish.
cons: Foam less energetic than top rivals

name: Brooks Hyperion Elite 5
description: The Hyperion Elite 5 updates Brooks's carbon racer with a more energetic midsole compound derived from the DNA Gold work in the Elite PB project. It is a 40mm-stack marathon shoe for racers who want Brooks's firmer, more controlled take on the super shoe.
pros: Improved foam energy return over the Elite 4
cons: Still trails the bounciest super shoes

name: Brooks Hyperion Elite 6
description: The Hyperion Elite 6 is Brooks's latest carbon-plated marathon racer, building on the Elite 5 with updated foam and a refined plate geometry. It aims squarely at race day, offering a light, stable platform at the legal 40mm stack limit.
pros: Light and stable at marathon pace
cons: Brooks racers remain a step behind the podium favorites in foam bounce

name: Brooks Hyperion Max 3
description: The Hyperion Max 3 is Brooks's super-trainer: a higher stack of DNA Flash v2 with the SpeedVault plate and a rapid-roll rocker. It bridges the gap between daily trainer and race shoe, handling tempos, long workouts, and even race day for runners who don't want a full carbon racer.
pros: Fast, rockered ride with plate assistance

name: Brooks Hyperion Max 4
description: The Hyperion Max 4 refines Brooks's plated super-trainer with DNA Flash v2 foam, the SpeedVault plate, and an aggressive rocker. It is the pick for uptempo long runs and workouts when you want speed-shoe geometry with trainer durability.
cons: Not as cushioned as rival super trainers

name: Brooks Launch 12
description: The Launch 12 is Brooks's budget-friendly lightweight trainer: a firm, snappy DNA foam midsole in a stripped-down package that can handle daily miles and pick up the pace. It is a good value pick for runners who like a simple, responsive ride without plates or big stacks.
pros: Light enough for strides and tempos
cons: Basic upper and outsole compared to pricier trainers

name: Brooks Revel 8
description: The Revel 8 is Brooks's entry-level do-everything trainer with a simple DNA foam midsole and a knit-style upper that works as well for the gym as the road. It gives newer runners a firm, predictable ride at a wallet-friendly price.
pros: Versatile for running and gym use
cons: Less durable outsole than pricier Brooks trainers

name: Brooks Revel 9
description: The Revel 9 continues Brooks's budget trainer line with updated DNA foam and a cleaner knit upper. It is a firm, no-frills shoe for shorter daily runs, new runners, and anyone who wants one affordable shoe for running and everything else.

name: Brooks Revel Max 2
description: The Revel Max 2 brings max-stack cushioning to Brooks's budget line, stacking soft DNA foam under a simple knit upper. It is a value-focused high-cushion cruiser for easy miles and runners who want big-shoe comfort without a big-shoe price.
pros: Max cushion at a mid-range price
Comfortable for walking and easy runs
cons: Foam is less lively than premium Brooks midsoles

name: Diadora Gara Carbon
description: Diadora's Italian-made carbon racer with a nitrogen-infused Anima midsole and full-length carbon plate. It rides firmer and slightly heavier than mainstream super shoes but offers standout build quality and a stable, controlled race-day platform.
pros: Stable, controlled ride for a super shoe
cons: Heavier and firmer than top carbon racers

name: Hoka Arahi 8
description: The Arahi 8 is Hoka's everyday stability trainer, using the firm J-Frame EVA rail along the medial side to guide overpronation without a rigid post. It rides softer and taller than most stability shoes thanks to the Hoka platform. A sensible pick for runners who need support but hate the feel of traditional motion-control shoes.
pros: J-Frame guidance without a harsh medial post
cons: Ride is unexciting for faster days

name: Hoka Arahi 9
description: The Arahi 9 continues Hoka's J-Frame approach to stability, pairing a supportive medial frame with the brand's tall, rockered cushioning. It is aimed at overpronators who want daily-mileage support that still feels like a modern cushioned trainer. Changes over the Arahi 8 are incremental, centered on the upper and fit.
cons: Not a shoe for tempo work
Little changed from the previous version

name: Hoka Bondi 10
description: The Bondi 10 carries forward the supercritical EVA platform introduced in the Bondi 9 with an updated upper and modest refinements. It remains Hoka's plushest everyday shoe: a tall, wide, deeply cushioned cruiser for easy miles and long days on your feet. Like every Bondi, it prioritizes protection over speed.
pros: Stable for such a tall shoe
cons: Still one of the heavier trainers around

name: Hoka Bondi 9
description: The Bondi 9 finally swaps in a supercritical EVA midsole, making Hoka's max-cushion cruiser noticeably softer and bouncier than the Bondi 8. It is built for recovery days, high-mileage heel strikers, and bigger runners who want maximum protection. The trade-off is weight and a ride that never wants to go fast.
pros: Softer supercritical foam is a real upgrade
Very protective for recovery days and big runners
cons: Sluggish at anything faster than easy pace

name: Hoka Cielo X1 2.0
description: The Cielo X1 2.0 is Hoka's flagship carbon marathon racer, cutting over an ounce from the original with dual layers of bouncy PEBA foam around a winged carbon plate. The ride is aggressive and rocker-heavy, rewarding midfoot strikers with a strong toe-off. It is one of the bounciest super shoes available, at one of the highest prices.
pros: Huge PEBA bounce with an aggressive rocker
Much lighter than the original Cielo X1
cons: Aggressive geometry punishes slow paces and heel striking

name: Hoka Cielo X1 3.0
description: The Cielo X1 3.0 carries forward Hoka's top-tier marathon racer formula: dual PEBA foam layers, a winged carbon plate, and an extreme rocker built for committed race pace. Updates over the 2.0 are iterative, aimed at fit and small weight savings. It stays a race-day-only tool for runners chasing PRs from 10K to the marathon.

name: Hoka Clifton 10
description: Hoka's flagship daily trainer got taller and moved to an 8mm drop in this version, with a compression-molded EVA midsole that stays soft without feeling mushy. It is the shoe most Hoka runners reach for on easy and moderate miles. Nothing about it is fast, but almost everything about it is comfortable.
pros: Soft, protective ride for daily miles
cons: Too much shoe for speed work

name: Hoka Clifton 11
description: The newest Clifton keeps the tall, soft EVA platform and 8mm drop of the Clifton 10 with a refined upper and small weight savings. It remains the definition of an easy-day cruiser: cushioned, rockered, and unfussy. Runners wanting pop or ground feel should look elsewhere in the lineup.
pros: Works for walking and standing all day too
cons: Midsole foam is ordinary EVA at this price

name: Hoka Gaviota 6
description: The Gaviota 6 is Hoka's max-cushion stability shoe, combining a broad platform, H-Frame support structure, and deep, soft foam. It targets overpronators and heavier runners who need more shoe than the Arahi offers. Think of it as a Bondi with guidance built in: very protective, not remotely fast.
pros: Great for bigger runners and long easy days
cons: Feels ponderous at anything but easy pace

name: Hoka Kawana 2
description: The Kawana 2 is Hoka's run-to-gym crossover: a firmer EVA midsole with a flatter, more stable platform than the brand's pure running shoes. It suits new runners and fitness-class regulars who want one shoe for treadmill miles, lifting, and errands. Dedicated runners will find better rides elsewhere in the lineup.
pros: Versatile for running plus gym work
cons: Firmer and heavier than Hoka's dedicated trainers
Unremarkable as a pure running shoe

name: Hoka Mach 6
description: The Mach 6 moved to a supercritical EVA midsole and became one of the best value daily trainers on the market: light, responsive, and happy at everything from easy runs to tempo. It is the pick in Hoka's lineup for runners who want one shoe that can do most things. Durability of the exposed midsole outsole sections is its main weakness.
pros: Light and responsive for the price
Handles easy miles and workouts alike
cons: Not plush enough for pure recovery days

name: Hoka Mach 7
description: The Mach 7 continues the supercritical EVA formula that made the Mach 6 a favorite, with an updated upper and slightly improved outsole coverage. It stays a light, versatile daily trainer that can pick up the pace without a plate. If the Clifton is Hoka's easy shoe, this is the do-everything one.
pros: Versatile from easy pace to tempo
Light for a full daily trainer
cons: Small price bump over the Mach 6
Still not the shoe for max-cushion lovers

name: Hoka Mach X 2
description: The Mach X 2 is Hoka's plated super-trainer: a tall PEBA midsole over a Pebax plate that gives it real pop for workouts and uptempo long runs while staying durable enough for training. It is the shoe for runners who want race-day feel without burning through a $275 racer. At nearly 9.5 ounces it is more trainer than racer.
pros: PEBA foam plus Pebax plate at a trainer price
Great for tempos and marathon-pace long runs
More durable than a true racer
cons: Tall stack can feel unstable in corners

name: Hoka Rincon 4
description: The Rincon 4 is Hoka's budget lightweight trainer: a simple EVA midsole, a minimal upper, and very little weight. It is a good value pick for runners who like a light, rockered shoe for daily miles and do not need premium foam. As always with the Rincon, the sparse outsole rubber wears faster than heavier trainers.

name: Hoka Rincon 5
description: The Rincon 5 keeps the line's formula intact: light EVA cushioning, a stripped-down upper, and a wallet-friendly price. It suits runners who want an unfussy lightweight trainer for daily miles and the occasional pickup. Expect the usual Rincon trade-off of low weight for shorter outsole life.
pros: One of the lightest trainers at this price
Nimble enough for strides and fartlek
cons: Foam and outsole durability remain average
Less cushioned feel than the stack number suggests

name: Hoka Skyflow
description: The Skyflow slots between the Clifton and Bondi with a supercritical EVA midsole that is softer and livelier than either shoe's foam at launch. It is a premium neutral daily trainer for runners who want plush cushioning that still transitions smoothly. It does not do anything flashy, it just rides well.
cons: Not light enough for real speed work

name: Hoka Skyflow 2
description: The Skyflow 2 keeps the supercritical EVA midsole that made the original a sleeper hit and updates the upper for a better lockdown. It remains Hoka's premium cushioned neutral trainer for daily miles and long runs. If you found the Clifton too basic and the Bondi too big, this is the middle path.
pros: Versatile across easy and steady paces
Improved fit over the first version
cons: Sits awkwardly between Clifton and Bondi price points
No plate or pop for workouts

name: Hoka Skyward X
description: The Skyward X is Hoka's biggest road shoe: a 48mm stack of supercritical EVA and PEBA with a convex carbon plate sandwiched in between. The plate here is for smoothing the rocker, not for racing — this is a plush, bouncy cruiser for long easy runs. It is heavy and expensive, but nothing else in the lineup feels this cushioned.
pros: Carbon plate smooths the rolling ride
Surprisingly stable for the stack height

name: Hoka Skyward X 2
description: The Skyward X 2 refines Hoka's super-stacked cruiser, keeping the dual-foam midsole and rocker-shaping carbon plate while trimming a little weight. It remains a max-max-cushion shoe for long, easy miles rather than a racer. Runners who love the original's marshmallow ride get more of the same.
pros: Deepest cushioning in Hoka's road line
Plate-driven rocker keeps the heavy shoe rolling

name: Mizuno Neo Vista 2
description: Mizuno's super-trainer stacks a huge slab of bouncy Enerzy NXT foam around a flexible nylon Wave plate, topped with a stretchy knit bootie upper. It's a fun, highly cushioned option that can handle everything from easy days to uptempo long runs.
cons: Knit upper runs warm and less secure
Tall stack feels unstable on tight corners

name: Mizuno Neo Vista 3
description: The third Neo Vista continues Mizuno's max-stack super-trainer recipe: springy Enerzy NXT foam, a flexible nylon plate, and a knit upper. It remains one of the most versatile high-cushion trainers for runners who want one shoe for most of the week.
pros: Handles tempo work despite the stack
cons: Bootie fit won't suit wide feet

name: Mizuno Neo Zen
description: A plateless sibling to the Neo Vista, the Neo Zen delivers a full stack of soft, bouncy Enerzy NXT foam in a surprisingly light package. It's an easy recommendation for runners who want max-cushion fun without a plate or a super-trainer price.
pros: Good value in the max-cushion class

name: Mizuno Neo Zen 2
description: The second Neo Zen keeps the plate-free Enerzy NXT midsole that made the original a sleeper hit, with refinements to the upper and outsole. It stays a light, soft, everyday cruiser for runners who like a bouncy ride at a fair price.

name: Mizuno Wave Inspire 21
description: Mizuno's stability counterpart to the Wave Rider uses a fan-shaped Wave plate instead of a hard medial post to guide overpronators. Enerzy foam keeps the ride reasonably lively for a support shoe, and the 12mm drop favors heel strikers who need daily guidance.

name: Mizuno Wave Inspire 22
description: The latest Inspire continues Mizuno's plate-based approach to stability, steering the foot with a fan-shaped Wave plate and Enerzy foam rather than a rigid post. A sensible pick for heel-striking overpronators who want traditional structure in a daily trainer.
cons: Not a light or fast shoe

name: Mizuno Wave Rebellion Flash 2
description: A plated tempo shoe that pairs Enerzy Lite foam with a glass-fiber-reinforced plate for snappy workouts and shorter races. It's more forgiving and more traditional than the Rebellion Pro, making it the Mizuno speed shoe most runners can actually use.
pros: Snappy plated ride at trainer price
Versatile from intervals to race day
More accessible than the Rebellion Pro
cons: Outclassed by super shoes for marathons

name: Mizuno Wave Rebellion Pro 3
description: Mizuno's marathon racer uses a radical cutaway heel geometry, Enerzy Lite Plus foam, and a carbon-infused plate to push runners onto their midfoot. It rewards efficient midfoot and forefoot strikers with an aggressive, fast ride, but heel strikers should look elsewhere.
pros: Extremely aggressive rocker for fast racing

name: Mizuno Wave Rebellion Pro 4
description: The fourth Rebellion Pro refines Mizuno's distinctive cutaway-heel racing geometry with updated Enerzy Lite Plus foam and a stiff carbon-infused plate. It remains a specialist marathon shoe for midfoot strikers chasing fast times rather than an everyman racer.

name: Mizuno Wave Rider 29
description: Mizuno's long-running neutral daily trainer pairs Enerzy NXT foam with the signature Wave plate for a smooth, slightly firm heel-to-toe ride. The high 12mm drop and stable rearfoot make it a natural fit for heel strikers logging everyday miles.
cons: High drop won't suit low-drop fans

name: Mizuno Wave Rider 30
description: The 30th edition of Mizuno's flagship daily trainer keeps the Enerzy NXT midsole and Wave plate formula that made the Rider a staple. It remains a balanced, durable pick for runners who want structure and a traditional high-drop feel over marshmallow softness.
cons: Not soft enough for recovery-day lovers

name: Mizuno Wave Sky 10
description: The tenth Wave Sky keeps the formula of a big Enerzy NXT stack on a broad, forgiving platform built for recovery days. It trades speed for comfort and durability, making it a strong pick for heavier runners piling up easy mileage.
cons: One of the heavier max trainers

name: Mizuno Wave Sky 9
description: Mizuno's max-cushion cruiser stacks soft Enerzy NXT over a wide, stable platform for easy days and long, slow miles. It's a plush but substantial shoe that suits bigger runners and heel strikers who want protection over pop.
pros: Stable base for a max shoe

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X 1080 v14
description: New Balance's flagship cruiser, built on a full slab of soft Fresh Foam X with a gentle rocker. The v14 got a touch heavier and softer than the v13, making it best for easy miles, long runs, and recovery days rather than anything fast. A roomy, plush knit upper makes it an easy shoe to live in every day.
pros: Plush, protective ride for easy days
cons: Too soft and slow for workouts

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X 1080 v15
description: The latest version of New Balance's premium max-cushion daily trainer, still centered on a thick, soft Fresh Foam X midsole and rockered ride. The v15 trims a bit of weight from the v14 while keeping the same plush, easy-mile character. It remains a comfort-first shoe for daily miles, long runs, and recovery days.
pros: Accommodating fit with wide sizes available

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X 860 v14
description: The 860 is New Balance's traditional stability workhorse, and the v14 modernizes it with a taller Fresh Foam X midsole and a broad, guided platform. It gives overpronators dependable daily support with a firmer, more traditional ride than the Vongo. Durable and secure, it is built for steady mileage rather than speed.
pros: Secure, traditional fit with width options
cons: Firm ride compared with plusher rivals

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X 860 v15
description: The newest 860 continues as New Balance's structured daily trainer for runners who need medial support. It carries forward the v14's Fresh Foam X platform and guidance geometry with a refreshed upper and minor weight savings. A steady, durable pick for overpronators logging everyday miles.
cons: Not a lively or fast ride

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X 880 v15
description: The 880 is New Balance's no-drama neutral workhorse, with a balanced Fresh Foam X midsole that is neither mushy nor harsh. The v15 keeps the formula: durable outsole, secure mesh upper, and a predictable ride that handles daily miles for years of versions. It is the sensible pick for runners who want one reliable shoe for most of their running.
pros: Fits a wide range of feet with width options

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X 880 v16
description: The newest 880 continues the line's role as New Balance's straightforward neutral daily trainer on a balanced Fresh Foam X platform. Changes from the v15 are incremental: a slightly lighter build and refreshed upper rather than a redesign. Buy it for consistent, durable daily mileage, not for tempo days.
cons: Firmer and heavier than max-cushion options

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X Balos
description: Balos is New Balance's newest max-cushion trainer, slotting near the More with a tall, soft Fresh Foam X stack and a smooth rocker aimed squarely at comfort. It launched in 2025 as a plush option for recovery days and long, easy miles, with a wide base that keeps the soft foam from feeling tippy. A newer name, so it lacks the track record of the 1080 or More lines.
pros: Stable base for a max-stack shoe
cons: New model with limited long-term track record

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X More v5
description: New Balance's biggest-stack trainer, with a tall, wide slab of Fresh Foam X and a pronounced rocker to keep the huge platform rolling forward. The v5 is softer and smoother than earlier Mores and shines on recovery days and slow long runs, especially for bigger runners. The broad base gives it an inherently stable feel despite the height.
pros: Smooth rocker for a tall shoe
cons: Heavy and slow to turn over
Low 4mm drop can bother sensitive calves

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X More v6
description: The newest More keeps the formula of the v5: a very tall, very wide Fresh Foam X platform with a strong rocker, tuned for comfort above all. It is a recovery-day and easy-long-run specialist that suits runners who want maximum protection underfoot. Expect small refinements in weight and upper fit rather than a new ride.

name: New Balance Fresh Foam X Vongo v6
description: The Vongo v6 is New Balance's plush stability trainer, pairing a generous Fresh Foam X midsole with a very wide base and raised medial sidewalls instead of a hard post. Guidance comes from geometry, so it supports overpronators without feeling intrusive. A good choice for runners who want real support with modern, soft cushioning.
pros: Supportive without a harsh medial post
cons: Ride is too relaxed for faster days

name: New Balance FuelCell Propel v5
description: The Propel v5 is New Balance's budget-friendly energetic trainer, using an EVA-blend FuelCell midsole and a TPU plate to add some snap without the premium price. It is a solid one-shoe option for newer runners who want a bit of liveliness for daily miles and occasional pickups. The foam is not as bouncy as the Rebel's PEBA blend, but the value is hard to argue with.
pros: Versatile for daily miles and light workouts
cons: Foam is a step down from the Rebel
A bit heavy for true speed work

name: New Balance FuelCell Rebel v5
description: The Rebel v5 is a light, bouncy, plate-free speed trainer built on a PEBA-blend FuelCell midsole that got taller and softer than the v4. It is one of the most fun do-it-all fast shoes on the market, handling tempos, intervals, and even daily miles for lighter runners. No plate means it stays flexible and natural underfoot.
pros: Versatile from daily runs to workouts
cons: Less structure for runners who need support

name: New Balance FuelCell Rebel v6
description: The sixth Rebel continues the line's recipe of a light, unplated PEBA-blend FuelCell trainer that blurs the line between speed shoe and daily trainer. It carries forward the v5's tall, bouncy platform with small upper and outsole refinements. Ideal for runners who want one energetic shoe for workouts and quicker everyday miles.
pros: Bouncy FuelCell foam without a plate
Handles a wide range of paces
cons: Softness can feel unstable on tired legs

name: New Balance SC Elite 6
description: The next generation of New Balance's carbon-plated marathon super shoe, continuing the PEBA FuelCell and Energy Arc plate combination at the legal 40mm limit. It builds on the well-received v5 with incremental weight and foam tuning rather than a reinvention. A race-day-only tool for runners chasing PRs from 10K to the marathon.

name: New Balance SC Elite v5
description: New Balance's top marathon racer pairs a full PEBA FuelCell midsole with the brand's Energy Arc carbon plate and a 40mm stack. The v5 softened the ride and improved the turnover compared with the v4, making it a legitimate contender for marathon and half-marathon race day. It rewards a smooth midfoot strike and rested, faster legs.
pros: Bouncy PEBA foam with carbon Energy Arc plate
Light and smooth at race pace
More forgiving than many super shoes
cons: Low 4mm drop and soft stack are less friendly to heavy heel strikers

name: New Balance SC Pacer 3
description: The third SC Pacer keeps New Balance's short-distance racing formula: a moderate-stack FuelCell platform with an Energy Arc carbon plate for quick, aggressive turnover. It carries the v2's character forward with minor foam and upper refinements. Built for racing 5K through the half and for runners who prefer a lower, faster-feeling plated shoe.
pros: Light for hard sessions and short races
More stable than towering super shoes
cons: Not cushioned enough for most marathoners
Niche next to the SC Elite

name: New Balance SC Pacer v2
description: The SC Pacer v2 is New Balance's lower-stack carbon-plated racer for shorter, faster events. With a firmer FuelCell midsole and Energy Arc plate on a nimbler platform than the SC Elite, it is aimed at 5K to half-marathon racing and hard interval sessions. Runners who find 40mm super shoes squirmy will like its direct, connected feel.
pros: Excellent for 5K-10K racing and track-adjacent workouts
Lighter and more agile than max-stack racers
cons: Less protection for the full marathon
Firm ride is unforgiving on easy days

name: New Balance SC Trainer 4
description: The fourth SC Trainer continues as New Balance's plated super-trainer, carrying the FuelCell and Energy Arc formula of the v3 with modest weight savings and upper updates. It is designed for marathon-block long runs and workouts where you want carbon-plate efficiency in a durable package. A logical daily companion to the SC Elite for committed racers.

name: New Balance SC Trainer v3
description: The SC Trainer v3 is the training partner to the SC Elite: a high-stack FuelCell shoe with an Energy Arc carbon plate built to survive daily mileage. It trades some of the racer's aggression for a more stable platform and a durable outsole. Best for long runs and uptempo days when you want plated assistance without burning race shoes.
pros: Plated super-trainer ride at trainer durability
Protective high stack for long runs
More stable than the racing version

name: Nike Alphafly 3
description: The Alphafly 3 is Nike's flagship marathon racer, combining a full carbon Flyplate, ZoomX foam, and dual forefoot Air Zoom pods on a continuous single-piece midsole. It was the shoe under Kelvin Kiptum's world record and remains one of the most propulsive long-distance racers available. The tall, springy platform rewards rhythmical midfoot striking and is strictly a race-day tool.
pros: Propulsive Air pods plus carbon plate
More stable and smoother than Alphafly 2
cons: Ride is too specialized for training

name: Nike Alphafly 4
description: The Alphafly 4 continues Nike's max-tech marathon racer formula: ZoomX foam, a full-length carbon Flyplate, and forefoot Air Zoom units at the 40mm legal limit. Expect the same aggressive, bouncy propulsion as the 3 with updated geometry and upper. It exists for one job, racing 10K to the marathon as fast as possible.
cons: Not durable enough for regular training

name: Nike Downshifter 13
description: The Downshifter 13 is Nike's entry-level running shoe, with simple EVA cushioning and a breathable mesh upper at a budget price. It works for new runners logging short, easy miles and doubles as a gym or walking shoe. The basic foam and modest stack mean experienced runners will outgrow it quickly.
pros: Fine for gym and casual miles
cons: Not built for high mileage or long runs

name: Nike Downshifter 14
description: The Downshifter 14 updates Nike's budget staple with a refreshed upper over the same simple EVA midsole formula. It remains a starter shoe for casual runners, walkers, and gym-goers who want the swoosh under $100. Serious mileage calls for a Winflo or Pegasus instead.
pros: Versatile for gym and casual use
cons: Durability and cushioning limits for real training

name: Nike Flex Experience 13
description: The Flex Experience 13 is a flexible, minimal budget shoe with deep flex grooves and a thin EVA midsole, sitting at the very bottom of Nike's running range. It is best for short jogs, gym sessions, and all-day wear rather than structured training. Runners logging real mileage will want more cushioning and support.
cons: Thin cushioning unsuitable for long runs

name: Nike Pegasus 41
description: Nike's flagship daily trainer moved to full-length ReactX foam with dual Air Zoom units in the 41, giving a snappier, slightly softer ride than the 40. It remains the do-everything workhorse for easy miles, tempo days, and long runs alike. Not the plushest or the fastest shoe in the lineup, but it fits most feet and rarely misses.
pros: ReactX foam is bouncier than past Pegasus foam
cons: Not exciting for dedicated speed work

name: Nike Pegasus 42
description: The latest Pegasus keeps the ReactX midsole and dual Air Zoom units of the 41 with a refined upper and small fit tweaks. It stays true to the line's identity: a durable, moderately cushioned daily trainer that handles everything from easy days to steady long runs. Runners wanting maximum softness or a super-light ride should look elsewhere in Nike's range.

name: Nike Pegasus Plus
description: Essentially the successor to the Pegasus Turbo, the Pegasus Plus pairs a full-length ZoomX midsole with a stripped-down Flyknit upper. It is a light, energetic trainer that livens up uptempo days and shorter races without a plate. The thin upper and price put it in enthusiast territory rather than everyday-value territory.
pros: Full ZoomX ride at a trainer height
Light and versatile for tempo work
cons: ZoomX outsole coverage wears faster than the standard Pegasus

name: Nike Pegasus Plus 2
description: The second Pegasus Plus continues the formula of full-length ZoomX foam in a light, plate-free trainer built for faster daily miles. Expect the same energetic, flexible ride as the original with an updated upper for a more secure lockdown. It sits between the standard Pegasus and Nike's plated speed shoes in both feel and price.

name: Nike Pegasus Premium
description: The Pegasus Premium stacks ZoomX, a full-length sculpted Air Zoom unit, and ReactX into the tallest, bounciest Pegasus ever made. The ride is fun and highly cushioned for long cruisy miles, but all that tech makes it noticeably heavy. It is a max-stack experience shoe, not a racer, and the price reflects the tech rather than pure performance.
pros: Visible full-length Air Zoom gives a lively ride

name: Nike Pegasus Premium 2
description: The second Pegasus Premium keeps the ZoomX-plus-Air-Zoom-plus-ReactX sandwich that defines the model, trimming a little weight and cleaning up the upper. It remains a plush, springy max-stack cruiser for runners who want the most dramatic Air-cushioned ride Nike makes. Still heavy and expensive relative to simpler trainers that cover the same runs.
cons: High price for a non-racing trainer

name: Nike Quest 6
description: The Quest 6 slots just above the Revolution in Nike's budget range, adding a bit more midsole and a more structured upper for everyday easy running. It is a serviceable, no-frills trainer for beginners and low-mileage runners. The foam is plain EVA, so the ride is firm and utilitarian rather than plush or springy.
pros: Secure fit for a budget shoe

name: Nike Quest 7
description: The Quest 7 continues Nike's budget trainer line with simple EVA cushioning and a supportive mesh upper for everyday easy running. It targets beginners and casual runners who want a slightly more substantial shoe than the Revolution. Expect dependable but unremarkable performance.
cons: Not suited to long or fast running

name: Nike Revolution 7
description: The Revolution 7 is Nike's cheapest running shoe, a soft-ish EVA cruiser aimed at beginners, walkers, and everyday wear. It is comfortable enough for short easy runs and is one of the best-selling shoes in the world on price alone. There is no advanced foam or structure here, and it shows on longer or faster efforts.
pros: Comfortable for walking and short runs

name: Nike Revolution 9
description: The Revolution 9 keeps Nike's entry-level formula intact: a simple EVA midsole, breathable mesh, and a price most trainers cannot touch. It suits brand-new runners and anyone who mostly walks but wants a shoe that can jog. Runners training regularly should step up to the Winflo or Pegasus tiers.
pros: One of the cheapest real running shoes
cons: Basic foam bottoms out on longer runs

name: Nike Rival Fly 5
description: The Rival Fly 5 is Nike's budget speed shoe, a low-slung lightweight trainer-racer with Cushlon foam and a forefoot Zoom Air unit. It is popular with high school and college runners as an affordable workout and race option without super-shoe pricing. The traditional low stack gives good ground feel but little protection for long distances.

name: Nike Streakfly 2
description: The Streakfly 2 is Nike's short-distance road racer, a featherweight ZoomX shoe built for the 5K and 10K where ground feel and turnover beat max stack. A midfoot plate adds some snap without the stiffness of a full carbon racer. It is a specialist: fantastic for short races and intervals, undercushioned for most runners beyond 10K.
cons: Too little cushion for long races
Niche use case for the price

name: Nike Structure 26
description: The Structure 26 is Nike's traditional stability trainer, using a firmer medial midsole and a wide, guided platform to keep overpronators tracking straight. Updated foam softens the ride compared with older Structures while keeping the supportive character. It is the Nike answer to the Adrenaline GTS and GT-2000 for runners who need real medial support.
cons: Heavier and stiffer than neutral peers
Support feel is unnecessary for neutral runners

name: Nike Structure 27
description: The Structure 27 refines Nike's core stability trainer with the same guided, medially supported platform and a slightly updated fit. It remains the go-to Nike for runners who overpronate and want a durable daily shoe with real guidance. Neutral runners will find the ride firmer and more controlled than they need.

name: Nike Structure Plus
description: The Structure Plus brings Nike's premium-foam treatment to its stability line, pairing a taller, softer midsole with a wide guided base and medial support. It targets overpronators who want max-cushion comfort for long and easy miles instead of the firmer standard Structure. As a Plus-tier shoe it carries extra weight and a higher price.

name: Nike Vaporfly 4
description: The Vaporfly 4 trims weight from an already legendary racer, pairing ZoomX foam with a full carbon plate in a lower, nimbler package than the Alphafly. It is arguably the most versatile super shoe Nike makes, at home from 5K to the marathon and light enough for hard workouts. The narrow racing fit and thin upper are all business.
cons: Narrow fit will not suit wide feet

name: Nike Vomero 18
description: The Vomero 18 grew into a true max-cushion trainer, stacking soft ZoomX over a stable ReactX base at 46mm in the heel. It delivers one of the best plush-ride values on the market at $150, ideal for recovery days, easy miles, and heavier runners who want protection. It is not light or fast, and it does not pretend to be.
pros: ZoomX over ReactX is soft yet stable
cons: Too much shoe for speed work

name: Nike Vomero 19
description: The Vomero 19 carries forward the ZoomX-over-ReactX max-cushion recipe that made the 18 a hit, with an updated upper and minor ride refinements. It stays the value pick in Nike's plush tier: deep, protective cushioning for easy days and long runs at a sane price. Runners chasing a lighter or snappier shoe should stay in the Pegasus family.
pros: Strong value in the max-cushion class

name: Nike Vomero Plus
description: The Vomero Plus swaps the standard model's dual-foam stack for full-length ZoomX, making it the softest and bounciest shoe in the Vomero family. It is a plush cruiser for long runs and easy days that still feels lively thanks to the all-ZoomX midsole. Softness comes at the cost of some inherent stability, so runners who need a steadier platform may prefer the Vomero 18 or 19.
pros: Full ZoomX midsole is soft and bouncy
cons: Soft platform can feel unstable in corners
ZoomX midsole durability is only average

name: Nike Vomero Premium
description: Nike's tallest trainer, the Vomero Premium piles ZoomX and large Zoom Air units into a towering max-stack platform aimed at ultimate long-run comfort. The ride is enormous, soft, and surprisingly bouncy, but the shoe is heavy and the price is steep. It is for runners who want the most cushioning Nike sells and do not care about the scale.
pros: Bouncy Air-assisted ride for its size
cons: Too tall and soft for faster running

name: Nike Winflo 11
description: The Winflo 11 is Nike's mid-budget daily trainer, combining Cushlon foam with a full-length Air Zoom unit for a firm but smooth ride. It covers easy miles reliably and holds up well for the price. The foam is basic compared with ReactX or ZoomX, so it suits newer runners and value shoppers more than performance seekers.

name: Nike Winflo 12
description: The Winflo 12 continues the line's role as Nike's dependable budget-plus trainer, with cushioned foam, a full-length Air Zoom unit, and a refreshed upper. It is built for everyday easy running and gym-to-road versatility rather than performance. A sensible pick for runners who want a real running shoe without flagship pricing.

name: Nike Zoom Fly 6
description: The Zoom Fly 6 is Nike's super trainer: a ZoomX core wrapped in a firmer SR-02 carrier with a full carbon Flyplate. It gives much of the plated race-day feel in a more durable, more stable package for tempo runs, marathon-pace work, and even racing on a budget. Heavier than a true super shoe, it is the training partner to the Vaporfly rather than a replacement.
pros: Carbon-plated ride at a trainer price

name: Nike Zoom Fly 7
description: The Zoom Fly 7 carries on as Nike's plated super trainer, with a carbon Flyplate and ZoomX-cored midsole tuned for workouts and long marathon-pace efforts. It keeps the durable, do-the-hard-training role that made the 6 popular, with fit and foam refinements. Still the sensible pick for runners who want one plated shoe for both training and racing.
cons: Not as light or bouncy as a true racer
Firm carrier foam dulls the ZoomX feel

name: On Cloudboom Strike
description: On's full-length carbon super shoe with a tall Helion HF PEBA midsole, worn to major marathon wins. The ride is soft and rockered with a snug, race-specific fit. It rewards efficient midfoot strikers more than heel strikers.
pros: Soft, fast PEBA and carbon setup

name: On Cloudboom Strike 2
description: The second generation of On's carbon-plated marathon racer, keeping the tall Helion HF PEBA stack and aggressive rocker of the original. Expect small refinements to the upper and geometry rather than a rework. Still a snug-fitting shoe aimed at efficient racers.

name: On Cloudboom Strike LightSpray
description: The Cloudboom Strike platform topped with On's robot-sprayed, laceless LightSpray upper, cutting the shoe to around 170 grams. It is one of the lightest marathon super shoes available, with the same carbon plate and Helion HF foam underneath. The minimal upper fits like a sock and offers little adjustability.
pros: Exceptionally light for a marathon shoe
Same fast plate and foam as the Strike
cons: No laces means no fit adjustment

name: On Cloudeclipse
description: On's max-cushion daily trainer with a double layer of CloudTec Phase pods and a Speedboard for structure. The ride is soft yet surprisingly stable thanks to the wide base, making it a strong pick for long easy miles. One of the more accessible-feeling shoes On makes.
pros: Handles long runs and recovery days well

name: On Cloudmonster 2
description: On's biggest CloudTec trainer, with oversized Helion-foam pods and a pronounced rocker for easy and long miles. It rides softer and smoother than the original but stays on the heavy side for a daily shoe. Best for runners who want a protective cruiser rather than anything fast.
pros: Smooth rockered ride for long miles

name: On Cloudmonster 3
description: The third generation of On's max-pod cruiser keeps the big CloudTec elements and rocker geometry while trimming a little weight. It remains a protective, smooth daily and long-run shoe rather than a fast one. A safe update for Cloudmonster fans.
cons: Still heavy for a daily trainer

name: On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper LightSpray
description: A premium super-trainer that pairs the Cloudmonster Hyper's PEBA-based Helion HF midsole with On's robot-sprayed LightSpray upper. The one-piece upper cuts weight but offers minimal structure, so it suits efficient runners on uptempo long runs. Very expensive for a trainer.
pros: Very light for its cushion level
cons: Minimal upper structure won't suit everyone

name: On Cloudmonster Hyper
description: A super-trainer take on the Cloudmonster with a PEBA-based Helion HF midsole and no plate. It is noticeably bouncier and lighter than the standard Cloudmonster, suiting uptempo long runs and marathon-pace work. Pricey for a plateless trainer.
pros: Much lighter than the regular Cloudmonster

name: On Cloudrunner 2
description: A supportive, budget-friendlier On daily trainer with a wide base and gentle guidance elements rather than a firm medial post. Helion foam and CloudTec pods give a moderate, slightly firm ride that favors durability over excitement. A sensible pick for newer runners who want light support.

name: On Cloudsurfer 2
description: On's softest everyday trainer, built on collapsing CloudTec Phase pods and Helion foam rather than firm rubber-feeling pods of older Ons. The ride is smooth and gentle, better for cruising and recovery days than picking up the pace. Light for how cushioned it feels.

name: On Cloudsurfer 3
description: The third version of On's soft CloudTec Phase daily trainer, continuing the smooth, collapsing-pod ride of its predecessors. It stays a comfort-first shoe for easy miles and recovery days. Expect modest refinements to the upper and foam rather than a redesign.

name: On Cloudsurfer Max
description: The max-stack version of the Cloudsurfer, stacking more CloudTec Phase foam under a rockered platform. It delivers a plush, smooth ride for long easy runs and recovery days. Heavier and more expensive than the standard Cloudsurfer without adding versatility.
cons: Noticeably heavier than the regular Cloudsurfer

name: On Cloudsurfer Next
description: A slightly cheaper, lighter spin-off of the Cloudsurfer with the same CloudTec Phase midsole concept. It is a comfortable, unfussy daily trainer that leans soft and smooth over energetic. A good entry point to On's running line.
cons: Ride can feel flat at faster paces

name: Puma Deviate Nitro 3
description: A carbon-composite-plated super trainer with Nitro Elite foam that handles daily miles, long runs, and workouts alike. The PWRPLATE gives it snap without making the ride harsh at easy paces. One of the most versatile one-shoe-quiver options at its price.
pros: Plated pop at a fair price

name: Puma Deviate Nitro 4
description: The fourth Deviate Nitro continues the plated super-trainer formula with Nitro Elite foam and a PWRPLATE for versatile training. It remains a strong single-shoe option covering easy days through tempo work. Expect refinement over revolution versus version 3.
pros: Good value for a plated shoe
cons: Not as light as dedicated speed shoes

name: Puma Deviate Nitro Elite 3
description: Puma's more traditional carbon racer, with Nitro Elite foam and a full-length PWRPLATE in a lighter, less extreme package than the Fast-R. It is fast, relatively stable for a super shoe, and priced below most flagship racers. A strong pick from 5K to the marathon.
pros: Light and fast without extreme geometry
cons: Slightly less bounce than top-tier racers

name: Puma Deviate Nitro Elite 4
description: The fourth Deviate Nitro Elite keeps Puma's approachable carbon-racer formula: Nitro Elite foam, a full PWRPLATE, and a manageable geometry. It targets racers who want super-shoe speed without the instability of more extreme designs. Expect incremental foam and upper updates.
pros: Competitive price for a super shoe

name: Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 2
description: Puma's split-sole marathon racer with an exposed carbon PWRPLATE and Nitro Elite foam in a decoupled two-part midsole. The aggressive geometry drives strong forward roll for efficient racers. It ran on many podiums but is heavier than the best in class.

name: Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3
description: A computationally redesigned version of the Fast-R that stripped roughly two ounces from its predecessor while keeping the exposed carbon plate and Nitro Elite foam. Lab and race results made it one of the most talked-about marathon shoes of 2025. Very expensive and unapologetically race-only.
cons: One of the priciest racers on the market
Extreme design isn't for everyday runners

name: Puma ForeverRun Nitro 2
description: Puma's stability trainer, using a firmer Nitro foam frame around a softer core plus raised sidewalls instead of an old-school medial post. It guides the foot without feeling intrusive, making it a good pick for overpronators and heavier mileage. Solid rather than exciting.

name: Puma Magnify Nitro 2
description: Puma's max-cushion cruiser stacks a thick slab of Nitro foam for soft, protective easy miles. It suits recovery days and bigger runners who want plushness with dependable PumaGrip traction. Too heavy and soft for anything resembling speed.
pros: Good value for a max-cushion shoe

name: Puma Velocity Nitro 3
description: One of the best value daily trainers around, with nitrogen-infused Nitro foam and grippy PumaGrip rubber for well under most rivals' prices. The ride is balanced and reliable for everything from easy days to moderate long runs. Nothing flashy, just a workhorse.
cons: Ride is merely decent, not exciting

name: Puma Velocity Nitro 4
description: The fourth Velocity Nitro adds a touch more foam while keeping the line's honest daily-trainer character and excellent PumaGrip traction. It stays one of the strongest value picks in running shoes. A do-everything trainer for runners who don't want to overthink it.
pros: Comfortable for a range of runs

name: Reebok FloatZig 1
description: Reebok's return to serious running, pairing Floatride Energy foam with a zig-zag geometry midsole and outsole. It is a fun, well-priced neutral daily trainer that earned surprisingly strong reviews for its smooth, lively ride.
pros: Lively Floatride Energy foam at a fair price
cons: Modest stack offers less long-run protection

name: Salomon Aero Blaze 2
description: A lighter, more traditional daily trainer than the Aero Glide, with a moderate energyFOAM midsole and a smooth, slightly rockered ride. It handles everyday miles well and can pick up the pace for strides or light tempo work.
pros: Versatile weight for a daily trainer
cons: Foam feels ordinary next to supercritical rivals
Hard to find in US run specialty stores

name: Salomon Aero Glide 3
description: Salomon's max-cushion road cruiser with a tall slab of energyFOAM and a gently rockered ride. It is built for easy miles and long runs where comfort matters more than pace, with a wide base that keeps the high stack stable.
pros: Plush, protective cushioning for long easy miles
cons: Too much shoe for uptempo days

name: Salomon Aero Glide 4
description: The 2026 update to Salomon's max-cushion road trainer keeps the tall energyFOAM stack and rockered geometry while trimming a little weight and refining the upper. It remains an easy-day and long-run shoe for runners who want protection over pop.
pros: High, protective stack for recovery and long runs
cons: Salomon road shoes have limited retail presence in the US

name: Salomon Aero Volt 2
description: A lightweight, low-slung trainer with a firm, responsive energyFOAM midsole for runners who like ground feel. It shines for tempo runs, intervals, and shorter races without a plate, and doubles as a fast daily shoe for efficient runners.
cons: Too firm and thin for long easy runs
Heel strikers may find cushioning sparse

name: Salomon S/Lab Phantasm 2
description: Salomon's carbon-plated road marathon racer, pairing a supercritical PEBA-based foam with a full-length plate and an aggressive rocker. It is a legitimate super shoe from a brand better known for trail, with a firm, propulsive ride that rewards efficient form.
pros: Light and aggressive at race pace
cons: Narrow fit will not suit wide feet

name: Saucony Endorphin Elite 2
description: Saucony's no-compromise flagship racer, built on an aggressive slotted carbon plate and the brand's softest, highest-rebound foam (PWRRUN HG). It's tuned purely for marathon race day, with a propulsive forward tip that rewards committed, fast running. Overkill for training and too aggressive for easy miles.
pros: Very light for a max-stack racer
cons: Unstable and inefficient at slower paces

name: Saucony Endorphin Elite 3
description: The third-generation Elite, due August 2026, continues Saucony's top-of-the-line marathon racer with PWRRUN HG foam and an aggressive carbon plate at the maximum legal stack. Expect small weight and geometry refinements aimed at elite and serious amateur marathoners. Strictly a race-day tool.
pros: Built purely for fast marathon racing
cons: Too aggressive for most training runs

name: Saucony Endorphin Pro 4
description: Saucony's carbon-plated marathon racer, stacking a PWRRUN HG topsole over PWRRUN PB with a full-length carbon plate and SPEEDROLL geometry. The ride is firmer and more stable than the bounciest super shoes, which many runners prefer late in a marathon. A dependable racer from 10K to the marathon.
pros: More forgiving than most carbon racers for heel strikers
cons: Snug racing fit isn't for wide feet

name: Saucony Endorphin Pro 5
description: The 2026 update to Saucony's carbon racer pushes the stack toward the legal limit and softens the PWRRUN PB and PWRRUN HG combination for more bounce. It keeps the carbon plate and SPEEDROLL rocker that make the Pro line efficient over the full marathon. A more forgiving, modern super shoe than the Pro 4.
pros: Bouncier, taller ride than the Pro 4
cons: Narrow fit and tall stack demand a settled stride

name: Saucony Endorphin Speed 4
description: The benchmark plated super-trainer: a PWRRUN PB midsole with a flexible winged nylon plate and SPEEDROLL rocker. It's fast enough to race, forgiving enough for daily training, and remains one of the most versatile shoes in running. If you own one fast shoe that isn't a carbon racer, this is the default answer.
pros: Outstanding versatility from tempo to race day
Bouncy PEBA foam with a forgiving nylon plate
Light for how much shoe you get
cons: Jack of all trades, master of none
Upper runs slightly roomy for racing

name: Saucony Endorphin Speed 5
description: The current Endorphin Speed sticks with PWRRUN PB and the winged nylon plate while trimming weight and dialing in the fit. It remains the do-it-all workout shoe for runners who want super-shoe feel without super-shoe fragility or price. Handles tempos, intervals, long runs, and racing when you don't want a stiff carbon plate.
pros: Lighter and better-fitting than the Speed 4
cons: Not as explosive as a true carbon racer

name: Saucony Endorphin Speed 6
description: The next iteration of Saucony's flagship super-trainer, arriving August 2026 with the familiar PWRRUN PB midsole and flexible nylon plate. Expect incremental refinement of a formula that already defines the plated-trainer category. Built for workouts, long runs, and racing outside of goal marathons.
cons: Brand new, so little long-term feedback yet
Carbon racers are still faster on race day

name: Saucony Guide 18
description: The stability sibling of the Ride, using a PWRRUN+ midsole with Saucony's CenterPath geometry — a wide base, raised sidewalls, and subtle guidance instead of a hard medial post. It supports overpronators without feeling stiff or corrective. A friendly pick for runners who want unobtrusive support for daily miles.
pros: Works for neutral runners who like a stable base
